lines.note: Fodorai is hodorai, an amount or degree, exemplified by a price. Quantidade como de preço supplies that quantitative sense; the widened crop now includes the punctuation and column rule.
Item adds capacity or means, Poſibilidade, ou poſſe. The scan supports one s in the first word, not OCR's stray r; the two long s forms in poſſe are kept distinct from a beta-like ligature.

runs.text: Hum certo liuro q̃ enſina aeſcreuer.

lines.note: Fǒfacuxi names a book teaching writing. The short gloss does not securely identify its title beyond this printed name, so no speculative kanji title is imposed; the final escrever is fully visible after widening.
Fǒfan is hōhan, a rice dish with other foods. The following lines describe finely cut toppings and broth; this culinary context distinguishes it from a generic cooked-rice entry.

runs.text: miudamente cortados ſobre que botão Xiru, &

lines.note: The other foods are finely cut, and xiru, shiru or broth, is poured over them. Xiru is an embedded Japanese food term but appears italic here; it is not made upright merely because of its language.
Comem finishes the preparation-and-eating description. This isolated Portuguese verb remains a continuation, not a new dictionary entry.
Fôfei is hōhei, an offering involving cut paper pieces. Papelinhos retalhados e pegados describes the paper attached to a stick, elaborated in the next rows.

runs.text: na ponta de hum pao que com certas cerimoni-

lines.note: The paper pieces are attached at a stick's tip and used with prescribed ceremonies. Cerimoni- visibly continues to as below; its right edge was missing in the old crop.

runs.text: as ſe offerecem diante dos Camis.

lines.note: The offerings are presented before the kami. Camis is the Portuguese pluralized Japanese term and is italic in this line, consistent with the surrounding explanatory sentence.
Fôfen is hōhen, praise and blame, glossed home, soshiru. The damaged initial letter is F, not OCR B; both the Japanese gloss and the nearby repeated fôfen support it.
Louvando, ou murmurando explains praising or speaking ill. The r in murmurando is worn but supported by the remaining trace and the word; Cano fi- begins the Japanese example below.

runs.text: tono vyeni fôfen yoi, l, varui.

lines.note: Cano fitono vyeni fôfen yoi, or varui, concerns good or bad reports about that person. Vyeni is ue ni, and yoi/varui supplies the evaluative contrast mirrored in Portuguese.

runs.text: aquelle homem tratão, ou falão bem, ou mal.

lines.note: The Portuguese says that people discuss or speak well or badly of that man. It completes the hōhen example without requiring modernized Japanese syntax.

runs.text: O que em nome del Rei gouerna, ou

lines.note: Fofit is hofit-, a checked-coda form of a word for assisting government. The definition identifies someone governing on the king's behalf; the final t is not expanded to tsu in the transcription.
Depoem das cousas completes the administration-related gloss. Its printed spelling is retained even though modern Portuguese would suggest dispõe in this sense; the text is not silently modernized.

Fǒfo is the damaged printed heading for hōhō, barely or with difficulty, glossed yōyō. The last o has no secure accent here; NINJAL itself notes the impression appears Fǒfo despite its normalized Fǒfǒ entry. The third letter is f, not ſ.
The Portuguese describes getting away as if crawling, with scarcely enough strength. Fǒ- begins the repeated Japanese adverb across the line break.

runs.text: fǒ nigueta, l, fǒfǒno teide nigueta.

lines.note: Fǒfǒ nigueta, alternatively fǒfǒno teide nigueta, means escaping in a desperate or barely successful manner. Nigeta is coherent with the Portuguese Fugir; the two accented syllables in the example need not be forced onto the damaged heading.

runs.text: gir, ou acolherſe aßi deſta maneira.

lines.note: Gir completes Fugir, followed by acolherse assi desta maneira. This closes the example of escaping or taking refuge in that fashion.

Fofucu is hofuku, prostrating or crawling on the belly; farabai farabǒ is the accompanying native verb gloss. OCR Forucu and Faraba lose meaningful letters; the scan supports f and final i respectively.
The belly or chest is placed on the ground out of reverence. This establishes the prostration sense here, not simply crawling for locomotion.

runs.text: Offerecer algũa couſa ao Idolo, ou Tera.

lines.note: Fôga is hōga, giving an offering to an idol or temple. Tera is an embedded Japanese term in Portuguese; its italic appearance is retained.
Fôgani iru means joining the body of donors. The scan has a pilcrow before the example that OCR omitted; entering the number of those who give is completed in the next line.

runs.text: fazem eſmola pera algũa Tera, ou obra pia.

lines.note: The donors give alms toward a temple or pious work. Tera is again embedded and italic, while obra pia is a Portuguese category rather than another Japanese term.
Fôgachǒ is hōgachō, a donation register. Rol, ou livro identifies its function; Fô- starts the example of entering one's name in it.
Fôgachǒni tçuqu means being entered in the donation register. The Portuguese reflexive escreverse confirms registration, not physically sticking to a book.
Dos que dão esta esmola specifies the people entered in the register: those making this donation. This closes the previous example.
Fǒgacu is hōgaku, direction or quarter. Fitono yu begins a sentence about where someone goes, rather than music, another modern word with a similar reading.
Yuqu fǒgacuuo xiranu means not knowing the direction someone goes. The Japanese argument structure matches Não saber a parte; the long vowel in hōgaku remains as printed.
Pera onde vai alguem completes the directional definition. Pera is the historical Portuguese form and is not replaced with para.

runs.text: Iunto da barriga, ou vazio antre

lines.note: Fogami denotes the area by the lower belly or groin. The Portuguese vazio antre introduces a space between the thighs and abdomen, not an abstract emptiness.
As coxas e barriga identifies those boundaries. The scan shows barriga, with rr, rather than OCR bartiga; the paired anatomical terms make the correction meaningful.

runs.text: Couſa clara, ou lucida como lũa,

lines.note: Fogaracana is hogaraka na, clear or bright, exemplified by the moon. This physical clarity sense differs from the modern dominant cheerful-personality use.
Fogaracana chiye is clear wisdom or understanding. OCR Fogatacana is inconsistent with both the visible r and the adjective above; Saber claro supplies the intellectual extension.
Fogaracani is hogaraka ni, the adverbial form. Adu. explicitly marks it as an adverb, with its sense inherited from the preceding clarity entry.

runs.text: Altura da vela que conforme ao vẽto

lines.note: Fogaſa is hogasa, the height at which a sail is carried. The explanation refers to adjusting that height according to the wind, not to the sail's material or width.
The sail is raised or lowered. Fogaſauo mo- begins the corresponding example, with motçu continuing on the next row.

runs.text: Por, ou leuar a vela em certa altura.

lines.note: Motçu completes the Japanese expression for holding the sail at a certain height. The Portuguese gives setting or carrying the sail at that height; no extra noun is supplied.
Fogaxi is hogashi-, to pierce or make a hole. The Portuguese is Furar, not OCR Farar, and X. marks the regional use; its punctuation is kept with the upright label.

runs.text: Certa caſa, ou Zaxiqui que hà nas va-

lines.note: Fôgiǒ is hōjō, a room or building within a temple establishment. The embedded room word is Zaxiqui, zashiki, not OCR Zaeiqui; its italic styling in this Portuguese line is retained.
Varelas are the religious establishments in this account, and the room is compared with a refectory. Fô- begins the more specific hōjō no shitsu expression below.

runs.text: Caſa, ou cubiculo que ha den-

lines.note: Fôgiǒno xit is hōjō no shit-, a checked ending for shitsu. Portuguese casa ou cubiculo explains the room; the final den- continues dentro below.
Tro completes dentro, locating the cubicle inside the temple establishment. This short row remains part of the preceding definition.
Fogue is hoge-, to become holed or hollow. The regional X. is upright as printed; Itẽ introduces the hollow-tree example below, and the period is not assigned a separate italic run.

runs.text: Fazer ſe oco como aruore velha, &c.

lines.note: Fazer-se oco como arvore velha describes becoming hollow like an old tree. The historical aruore spelling and the source spacing are preserved.
Fǒgue is hōge, dismissing or casting someone off, glossed hanachi, kudasu. The end mark after alguem is a comma in the scan, not a word-breaking hyphen.

Fitouo fǒgueſuru means dismissing a person. The scan supports Fitouo, not Ficouo, and retains an accent over the first o of fǒgue; the final mark is a stop, not an unfinished continuation into column 2.
Fǒguen is hōgen, slanderous speech, explained as soxiru cotoba, words of blame. Soxiru is one word despite OCR's inserted space; it is not the directional word sō plus a separate verb.
Fǒgueqi is hōgeki, with foco foco giving the native spear terms. Dardos, ou lanças curtas describes darts or short spears, not an attack verb.
Fôgueta is hōgeta, the upper jaw or jawbones. Queixadas is partly affected by a crossing stain but remains the Portuguese word supported by the scan, not OCR queixdoſas.
Fogueta is hogeta, a ship's yard. The short first vowel distinguishes this nautical word from the preceding hōgeta for the jaw; Verga do navio confirms the sense.

runs.text: Fôguio. Von cuzzure. i, Teiuǒno xiqio.

lines.note: Fôguio is hōgyo, the sovereign's death, literally the honourable collapse in von cuzzure. Teiuǒno xiqio states the emperor's death explicitly; this is not an ordinary person's passing.
Morte del Rei completes the hōgyo definition. The Portuguese specifies the ruler and matches the honorific Japanese expressions above.

runs.text: Eſteira da vela, ou eſteira de pa-

lines.note: Fogomo is hogomo, a mat used as a sail. The scan supports a single headword rather than OCR Fogo mo; palha continues on the following row.
Lha completes palha: a straw mat serving as a sail. The definition concerns the sail's matting, distinct from the previous entry for the yard.

runs.text: Papeis borrados, ou que ja não apro-

lines.note: Fôgu denotes waste or spoiled papers. The Portuguese identifies papers no longer useful, not simply papers that have been erased clean for reuse.
The definition also includes corrected and blotted material. Enmẽdadas retains the old spelling and nasal abbreviation rather than being regularized to modern emendadas.

Fô. i. is hō-i, wealth and rank, glossed takara, kurai. The i is part of this headword, not the explanatory Latin i.; the printed internal separator is retained even though it can confuse automatic kana hints.
Fô i mini amaru means wealth and honours exceeding one's station or person. The i again belongs to hō-i; the Portuguese starts Abundar and supplies the intended sense below.
Dar completes Abundar: abounding in wealth and honours. This is the translation of the preceding Japanese example rather than a separate verb entry.

Fǒi is hōi, a kindly intention, literally kōbashii kokoro in the gloss. The dictionary uses fragrant figuratively for graciousness; the printed accent differs from the preceding wealth-and-rank entry.

runs.text: boa, & amoroſa vontade, ou obra de amor. S.

lines.note: The Portuguese gives a good and loving will or an act of love. Vontade, with a worn n, replaces OCR voitade; the final S. remains italic as a register label.

Fô. i. here is hō-i, the force or efficacy of religious law, glossed nori no isei. Its i is part of the Japanese compound, not an explanation marker, and the Portuguese efficacy wording confirms that sense.
Fô-i uo furù is hō-i o furū, displaying the teaching's authority. The grave-like accent on furù is left as the scan/OCR preserves it; it is not silently regularized to another long-vowel mark.
Cacia completes efficacia, with aparato adding display or impressive apparatus. Both belong to the religious-law sense, not the wealth sense above.
A further Fô. i. is hōi, religious rank, explicitly fôno curai. The second i, followed by a comma, is the actual explanatory marker; the first belongs to the heading.
Doutrina completes dignidade da lei, ou doutrina. This closes the rank entry and should not be joined to the following garment name.

runs.text: Certa laya de veſtido de nono compri-

lines.note: Foi is hoi, a long garment of cloth. Nono is the printed cloth term here; it is retained rather than changed to a more familiar Portuguese pano solely from expectation.

runs.text: do de mangas largas como de Chinas, que ves-

lines.note: The garment has wide sleeves like those of Chinese clothing. Ves- begins vestem, whose subject is supplied on the next line.

runs.text: tem por cima os que acompanhão aos Cũgues.

lines.note: The wearers are those accompanying the court nobles, Cũgues, and the garment is worn on top. The scan reads cima, not OCR cuma; Cũgues remains an embedded italic term rather than being normalized to upright type.
A separate Foi entry names coarse Korean cloths. Nonos is retained as printed, corresponding to nono above; Còrea is the historical geographical spelling.

runs.text: Certa dignidade de Bõzos, ou rapados.

lines.note: Fôin is hōin, a Buddhist clerical rank. Bõzos, or shaven religious, identifies the holders; the embedded Bõzos is italic in this line.

runs.text: Couſa de que ſe tem magoa, ou peſar,

lines.note: Foinai is hoi nai, regretful or disappointing. The Portuguese lists grief or sorrow about something and continues with longing below.
Ou saudades adds longing or missing something to the definition. This remains part of the hoi nai entry, not a separate Japanese expression.
Fǒiqi is hōiki, a kingdom or realm, with a literary/register label S. The terse Portuguese Reino does not warrant a more specific political interpretation.
Foiqin is hoikin, a wiping cloth or towel. The definition begins with cleaning and continues with the things wiped below.
The cloth is used to dust or wipe bowls and tables. Escudelas and mesas identify household vessels and surfaces, confirming a practical cleaning cloth.

Fôit denotes cruelty in this entry, followed by the compounds fǒit jaqen and qendõ fǒit. The damaged heading accent is less complete than the example's caron; it is left at the OCR reading rather than harmonized automatically.
Fǒit completes the second compound, with Idem referring to the same cruelty sense. The clear caron here is not evidence that every damaged accent above must be identical.
Foitǒ is hoitō, provisions or food, glossed kate and labeled as Buddhist usage. The first o is unaccented in this heading; the examples below have their own printed accents.
Fǒitǒ suru is begging for food. The Portuguese pedir mantimento introduces the door-to-door manner of asking described below.
Iunreini foitǒ is junrei ni hoitō, a pilgrim's request for food. OCR Iuuremi confuses n/u and n/m; the scan and the explicit peregrino in the next row support Iunreini.

runs.text: pedir. i, Eſmola pera hũ peregrino.

lines.note: The formula is explained as alms for a pilgrim. This supplies a direct semantic check on junrei in the preceding Japanese phrase.
Fôja is hōja, repayment or recompense, glossed mukui muku. The scan shows the circumflex matching NINJAL's lexical form, not the OCR caron; Võ- begins on, a favour, across the break.
Võuo fôja suru means repaying a favour. The faint circumflex is retained on fôja, and the Portuguese verb is Retribuir, not OCR Retribair.
Beneficios completes the object: the favours or benefits received. It is the Portuguese translation of on, not an additional Japanese term.

runs.text: Officios ſolennes que fazem os Bõzos.

lines.note: Fôji is hōji, solemn religious observances performed by Buddhist clergy. Bõzos remains italic as printed within the definition.
A separate verb Fôji, uru, ita means repaying or recompensing. Gouon begins the example's object, the honourable favour; the entry is not merged with the homophonous ritual noun.
Gouon uo fôzuru means repaying a favour. The Portuguese gives pagar os beneficios or retribuir; fōzuru is the verb form corresponding to fōji in the paradigm.
Buir completes retribuir. This short continuation ends the repayment example.
Fǒjin is hōjin, an honourable visit or communication, literally kōbashū tomurō in the gloss. The Portuguese explains a visit or message, not the modern legal term hōjin.

runs.text: por peßoa, ou carta honrando ao q̃ viſitou, ou

lines.note: The honour may be conveyed by a person or by letter. Honrando ao que visitou introduces the recipient of this respectful wording and continues below.
The recipient may have sent a message. Fǒjin catajiqenacu begins an expression of gratitude for the honourable visit or communication, continuing with the polite auxiliary below.

runs.text: Agradeço muito a viſita de voßa

lines.note: ſoro is soro, the polite auxiliary completing katajikenaku soro, not OCR toro. The gloss thanks the addressee for the visit; viſita has an i omitted by OCR viſta.
Mercè completes voßa mercè, the respectful address. The grave accent is visible; S. is retained as the register label, and Fojire below remains separate catchword furniture.
